contents.html: This report introduces the cryptographic accordion as a tweakable, variable-input-length strong pseudorandom permutation (VIL-SPRP) that is constructed from an underlying block cipher. An accordion facilitates the cryptographic processing of messages of various sizes while offering enhanced security compared to the approved block cipher modes of operation that are specified in the NIST SP 800-38 series. This report introduces associated terminology, outlines design requirements for accordions, and describes three categories of applications for them.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、基盤となるブロック暗号から構成される、トゥイーカブルで可変入力長の強擬似ランダム置換（VIL-SPRP）として、暗号アコーディオンを紹介します。アコーディオンは、さまざまなサイズのメッセージの暗号処理を容易にしつつ、NIST SP 800-38 シリーズで規定された承認済みのブロック暗号の動作モードに比べて強化されたセキュリティを提供します。本報告書は、関連する用語を導入し、アコーディオンの設計要件を概説し、アコーディオンの 3 つの応用カテゴリを説明します。

contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

contents.html: A mode of operation is a method that defines how a block cipher cryptographically processes (e.g., encrypts and/or authenticates) data beyond a single block length. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-38 series [2–10] specifies several modes that were submitted for NIST’s consideration from several different sources over many years to address a variety of security requirements and use cases.
contents.html_ja: 動作モードとは、ブロック暗号が、単一のブロック長を超えるデータをどのように暗号処理（たとえば、暗号化や認証）するかを定める方法です。米国国立標準技術研究所（NIST）の Special Publication（SP）800-38 シリーズ [2–10] は、さまざまなセキュリティ要件とユースケースに対応するために、長年にわたり複数の異なる提案元から NIST の検討に提出された、いくつかのモードを規定しています。

contents.html: NIST introduces the term cryptographic accordion — or simply accordion — to describe a technique constructed from an underlying block cipher that itself acts like a cipher on inputs of varying sizes. Thus, an accordion is simultaneously a cipher and a mode of the underlying block cipher. Formally, an accordion is defined as a tweakable, variable-input-length-strong pseudorandom permutation (VIL-SPRP) that is constructed from an underlying block cipher. NIST expects to develop one or more accordions with a generic proof of security.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、基盤となるブロック暗号から構成され、それ自体がさまざまなサイズの入力に対する暗号のように振る舞う技術を表すために、暗号アコーディオン、または単にアコーディオンという用語を導入します。したがって、アコーディオンは同時に、暗号であり、かつ基盤となるブロック暗号の動作モードでもあります。形式的には、アコーディオンは、基盤となるブロック暗号から構成される、トゥイーカブルで可変入力長の強擬似ランダム置換（VIL-SPRP）として定義されます。NIST は、汎用的な安全性証明を備えた 1 つ以上のアコーディオンを開発することを見込んでいます。

contents.html: The limitations of the current NIST modes were identified in NIST Internal Report (IR) 8459 [11] as part of NIST’s review process under the auspices of the NIST Crypto Publication Review Board.<sup>1</sup> NIST hosted the Third Workshop on Block Cipher Modes of Operation 2023<sup>2</sup> to discuss how to improve NIST’s modes portfolio, including desirable additional security features and a variety of proposed techniques. As a follow up, NIST hosted the NIST Workshop on the Requirements for an Accordion Cipher Mode 2024 [12] to 1) propose the development of an accordion as a comprehensive solution for a variety of cryptographic functionalities and 2) solicit feedback on the design requirements.<sup>3</sup>

contents.html: In this report, the cryptographic functions that may be constructed from an accordion are called derived functions. These derived functions can use the properties of the accordion to offer improved security, usage bounds, and functionality over existing modes. For example, a derived function for authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) could provide additional security properties compared to Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) [6], such as nonce-misuse resistance, support for short tags, nonce hiding, and key commitment. These features could make the accordion-based derived function a more robust choice than GCM for many cryptographic applications.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書では、アコーディオンから構成できる暗号関数を派生関数と呼びます。これらの派生関数は、アコーディオンの特性を利用して、既存のモードよりも優れたセキュリティ、使用上の限界、機能を提供できます。たとえば、関連データ付き認証付き暗号（AEAD）の派生関数は、ナンス誤用耐性、短いタグのサポート、ナンスの秘匿、鍵コミットメントなど、Galois/Counter Mode（GCM）[6] に比べて追加のセキュリティ特性を提供できます。これらの機能により、アコーディオンベースの派生関数は、多くの暗号アプリケーションにとって、GCM よりも堅牢な選択肢になりえます。

contents.html: Another benefit is that an accordion facilitates the conceptual separation of the enciphering from the functional roles of different types of inputs (e.g., confidential data, associated data, randomization values, and nonces). This separation should promote easier, faster, and simpler deployment compared to the ad hoc development of dedicated modes for specific functionalities and security features.
contents.html_ja: もう 1 つの利点は、アコーディオンによって、暗号化の処理と、種類の異なる入力（たとえば、機密データ、関連データ、ランダム化値、ナンス）の機能上の役割とを、概念的に切り離しやすくなることです。この分離により、特定の機能やセキュリティ機能のための専用モードを場当たり的に開発する場合に比べて、展開がより容易で迅速、かつ単純になるはずです。

contents.html: The notion of an accordion as a tweakable VIL-SPRP evolved from related terminology in the academic literature. The term strong pseudorandom permutation (SPRP) formally captures the idea that changing any bit of the input randomizes every bit of output for both the permutation and its inverse. The term enciphering mode describes a block cipher mode of operation that provides length-preserving encryption for variable input length (VIL) messages. The term tweakable enciphering mode indicates that the enciphering mode would take an additional input called a tweak, which was first introduced only in the context of a tweakable block cipher [13] (i.e., with fixed-length input).
contents.html_ja: トゥイーカブルな VIL-SPRP としてのアコーディオンという概念は、学術文献の関連用語から発展しました。強擬似ランダム置換（SPRP）という用語は、入力のどのビットを変えても、置換とその逆置換の両方で出力のすべてのビットがランダム化されるという考え方を形式的に表現したものです。暗号化モード（enciphering mode）という用語は、可変入力長（VIL）のメッセージに対して長さを保存する暗号化を提供するブロック暗号の動作モードを表します。トゥイーカブル暗号化モード（tweakable enciphering mode）という用語は、暗号化モードがトゥイークと呼ばれる追加の入力を取ることを示します。トゥイークは、当初はトゥイーカブルブロック暗号 [13]（すなわち、固定長入力のもの）の文脈でのみ導入されました。

contents.html: Some early works are CMC [14], EME [15], and the Hasty Pudding Cipher [16]. Several related design approaches have since emerged, such as AEZ [17], HCTR2 [18], Glevian and Vigornian [19], and Docked Double Decker [20]. There are also constructions based on other primitives (e.g., XChacha [21]) and tweakable block ciphers (e.g., Adiantum [22] and ZCZ [23]). Bellare and Rogaway’s encode-then-encipher encryption [24] is an example of a technique that could be applied to an accordion to achieve authenticated encryption. Another category of techniques that support variable input lengths is format-preserving encryption (FPE), though the input domain is usually small in this case. Moreover, NIST’s standard FF1 [10] for FPE, although AES-based, is expected to perform much less efficiently than a well-designed accordion.
contents.html_ja: 初期の研究には、CMC [14]、EME [15]、Hasty Pudding Cipher [16] があります。その後、AEZ [17]、HCTR2 [18]、Glevian と Vigornian [19]、Docked Double Decker [20] など、関連する設計アプローチがいくつか現れました。他のプリミティブ（たとえば、XChacha [21]）やトゥイーカブルブロック暗号（たとえば、Adiantum [22] や ZCZ [23]）に基づく構成もあります。Bellare と Rogaway の encode-then-encipher 暗号化 [24] は、アコーディオンに適用して認証付き暗号を実現できる技術の一例です。可変入力長をサポートする技術の別のカテゴリに、フォーマット保存暗号化（FPE）がありますが、この場合、入力の領域は通常小さくなります。さらに、FPE 向けの NIST 標準 FF1 [10] は、AES ベースではあるものの、適切に設計されたアコーディオンよりはるかに効率が低いと見込まれます。

contents.html: An accordion is one layer of a larger process for achieving a cryptographic functionality, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In particular, the underlying block cipher is the innermost layer, which is called by the accordion. The accordion is called by a derived function that defines how the accordion will be used but does not necessarily provide additional cryptographic processing of the inputs. For example, a derived function could provide AEAD functionality by encoding its inputs and providing them to the accordion. The derived function would then be called by an application, such as the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol for secure communication on the internet. One motivation for the development of an accordion is that it can support a variety of functionalities, which are currently met by ad hoc or dedicated modes of operation.
contents.html_ja: アコーディオンは、図 1 に示すように、暗号機能を実現するより大きなプロセスの 1 つの層です。特に、基盤となるブロック暗号は最も内側の層であり、アコーディオンから呼び出されます。アコーディオンは、アコーディオンをどう使うかを定めるものの、入力に対する追加の暗号処理を必ずしも提供しない派生関数から呼び出されます。たとえば、派生関数は、入力を符号化してアコーディオンに渡すことで、AEAD の機能を提供できます。派生関数はその後、インターネット上の安全な通信のための Transport Layer Security（TLS）プロトコルなどのアプリケーションから呼び出されます。アコーディオンを開発する動機の 1 つは、現在は場当たり的な、あるいは専用の動作モードで満たされているさまざまな機能を、アコーディオンがサポートできることです。

contents.html: The derived function layer will specify an encoding for the inputs to the accordion, and the accordion will specify the inputs for the block cipher. For an encryption application, the outer layer takes in the raw data to be encrypted and applies an encoding (e.g., by adding some integrity check bits). The shared secret or master key provided to the outer layer may be used directly as the encryption key for the accordion or to specify some new accordion key. Using any other inputs provided, the derived function layer defines a tweak for the accordion. The accordion tweak, encoded message, and accordion key are used to call the accordion encryption function. Within the accordion encryption, a block cipher key, which may be the same as the accordion key, is used to call the block cipher. The encoded message blocks are input to the block cipher encryption, and ciphertext blocks are returned. The accordion collects the ciphertext blocks into a single ciphertext, which is returned to the derived function.
contents.html_ja: 派生関数の層は、アコーディオンへの入力の符号化を指定し、アコーディオンは、ブロック暗号への入力を指定します。暗号化のアプリケーションでは、外側の層が、暗号化する生データを受け取り、符号化を適用します（たとえば、完全性チェック用のビットを追加します）。外側の層に与えられる共有シークレット鍵またはマスター鍵は、アコーディオンの暗号化鍵として直接使われることも、新しいアコーディオン鍵を指定するために使われることもあります。派生関数の層は、与えられたその他の入力を使って、アコーディオンのトゥイークを定めます。アコーディオンのトゥイーク、符号化されたメッセージ、アコーディオン鍵が、アコーディオンの暗号化関数の呼び出しに使われます。アコーディオンの暗号化の内部では、アコーディオン鍵と同じ場合もあるブロック暗号の鍵を使って、ブロック暗号を呼び出します。符号化されたメッセージのブロックがブロック暗号の暗号化に入力され、暗号文ブロックが返されます。アコーディオンは、暗号文ブロックを 1 つの暗号文にまとめ、それが派生関数に返されます。

contents.html: The usage bounds of many cryptographic techniques are limited by the “birthday bound,” where collisions (i.e., repetitions among a set of randomly generated data blocks) can be expected to occur. contents.html: Security bounds for primitives (e.g., an accordion or derived function) are typically given for a single user. Multi-user security considers how the security of these primitives changes as the number of independent users of the primitive gets larger. There are generic bounds on multi-user security, but a complete analysis requires consideration of how a given construction of a primitive affects its multi-user security (e.g., [27–36]).

contents.html: Some applications involve encrypting inputs that include the key or are derived from the key in some way. For example, when the operating system swaps the contents of some memory page to disk, the storage encryption mode being used could encrypt a copy of its own key. The security proofs of most chaining modes do not cover this use case; the property required to ensure security is called security against key-dependent inputs (KDI security) [37–39]. As shown in [39], it is impossible to construct a KDI-secure deterministic construction (e.g., the accordion) if there is no restriction on generating KDIs.
contents.html_ja: 一部のアプリケーションでは、鍵を含む、あるいは何らかの形で鍵から導出された入力を暗号化します。たとえば、オペレーティングシステムが、メモリページの内容をディスクにスワップする際、使用中のストレージ暗号化モードが、自らの鍵のコピーを暗号化する場合があります。ほとんどのチェーニングモードの安全性証明は、このユースケースを対象としていません。セキュリティを確保するために必要な性質は、鍵依存入力に対するセキュリティ（KDI セキュリティ）と呼ばれます [37–39]。[39] で示されているとおり、KDI の生成に制限がない場合、KDI に対して安全な決定的構成（たとえば、アコーディオン）を構築することは不可能です。

contents.html: While performance is not as critical as security, the better an accordion performs, the more useful it is likely to be. The most important platform is likely to be relatively powerful processors in desktop or laptop computers and those used in cloud environments with hardware AES support. Performance in dedicated hardware, field programmable gate arrays, and constrained devices is also worthwhile but is not NIST’s focus for an accordion.

contents.html: NIST requires all three accordions to support variable-length tweaks with some minimum bit length \(s_{min}\) and up to some maximum bit length \(s_{max}\). For some applications, NIST expects that the accordion will need to support tweaks with a large maximum length. For example, in order to efficiently construct an AEAD derived function from an accordion, the tweak will likely contain the AEAD’s associated data. The value for \(s_{min}\) should be at most that of the block size \(n\), and the value of \(s_{max}\) should be at least \(2^{48}\) bits. While some applications (e.g., storage encryption) can take advantage of more efficient processing for tweaks that are short and of a fixed length, supporting fixed-length tweaks alone is insufficient. An accordion must be capable of handling the full range of required tweak lengths, even if it optimizes for specific, fixed-length tweaks to enhance performance in certain use cases. The ability to process variable-length tweaks remains essential to ensure flexibility and compatibility across diverse applications.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、3 つのアコーディオンすべてが、最小ビット長 \(s_{min}\) 以上、最大ビット長 \(s_{max}\) 以下の可変長トゥイークをサポートすることを求めます。一部のアプリケーションでは、アコーディオンが最大長の大きいトゥイークをサポートする必要があると NIST は見込んでいます。たとえば、アコーディオンから AEAD 派生関数を効率的に構成するには、トゥイークに AEAD の関連データが含まれる可能性が高いです。\(s_{min}\) の値はブロックサイズ \(n\) 以下とし、\(s_{max}\) の値は少なくとも \(2^{48}\) ビットとすべきです。一部のアプリケーション（たとえば、ストレージ暗号化）では、短い固定長のトゥイークをより効率的に処理できますが、固定長のトゥイークだけをサポートするのでは不十分です。特定のユースケースで性能を高めるために特定の固定長トゥイークに最適化する場合でも、アコーディオンは必要なトゥイーク長の全範囲を扱える必要があります。多様なアプリケーション間で柔軟性と互換性を確保するには、可変長トゥイークを処理できることが引き続き不可欠です。

contents.html: This section describes the derived functions of an accordion for the following three categories of applications: AEAD, tweakable encryption, and deterministic authenticated encryption (DAE). Each of these functions will have some application-specific inputs along with the message and a key. The particular use case of the function motivates a set of properties that should be achieved. For example, AEAD by definition includes a means of data authentication, while tweakable encryption does not. The following subsections provide 1) some guidelines for each of the derived functions, 2) an indication of how the functions could be constructed out of an accordion, and 3) discussion of additional security considerations.

contents.html: An AEAD scheme uses a key, a nonce, and optional associated data to encrypt a plaintext into a ciphertext while authenticating the plaintext and associated data. One possible construction for authenticated encryption from an accordion is shown in Fig. 2. In this example, the accordion message consists of the plaintext padded with \(\tau\) fixed bits (zeros) to support authentication<sup>5</sup>, which is verified upon decryption (not depicted). This construction encodes the nonce and any associated data into the accordion tweak.
contents.html_ja: AEAD 方式は、鍵、ナンス、任意の関連データを使い、平文と関連データを認証しながら、平文を暗号文に暗号化します。アコーディオンから認証付き暗号を構成する方法の一つを、図 2 に示します。この例では、アコーディオンのメッセージは、認証をサポートするために \(\tau\) 個の固定ビット（ゼロ）で埋めた平文からなり<sup>5</sup>、復号時に検証されます（図示せず）。この構成は、ナンスと任意の関連データをアコーディオンのトゥイークに符号化します。

contents.html: In practice, it can be difficult to ensure that nonces are not repeated. Therefore, nonce misuse resistance is an important property for an AEAD scheme. If the nonce is encoded as part of the tweak, then the security definition of the accordion ensures that repetition of the tweak<sup>6</sup> imposes the smallest possible security loss. Accordions are deterministic, so any invocations of the accordion on the same input — including the same tweak — will result in the same output. Otherwise, each new invocation will appear to be randomly selected from the set of not-yet-seen outputs of the correct length from the accordion function.
contents.html_ja: 実際には、ナンスが繰り返されないことを確実にするのは難しい場合があります。したがって、ナンス誤用耐性は AEAD 方式にとって重要な特性です。ナンスをトゥイークの一部として符号化すれば、アコーディオンのセキュリティ定義により、トゥイークの繰り返し<sup>6</sup>によるセキュリティ上の損失が最小限に抑えられることが保証されます。アコーディオンは決定的であるため、同じトゥイークを含む同じ入力でアコーディオンを呼び出すと、常に同じ出力になります。それ以外の場合、新しい呼び出しのたびに、アコーディオン関数から得られる、まだ確認されていない正しい長さの出力の集合から、ランダムに選ばれたように見える出力が得られます。

contents.html: The AEAD and DAE derived functions both support authentication of the input data. The number of bits of authentication security is \(\tau\), which means that \(2^{-\tau}\) is the maximum allowable probability that any given invalid ciphertext will be accepted as valid. The value of \(\tau\) also indicates the minimum number of bits of ciphertext expansion. A derived function that supports authentication will specify the set of values that are allowed for \(\tau\), which may include options for small ciphertext expansion.
contents.html_ja: AEAD と DAE の派生関数はどちらも、入力データの認証をサポートします。認証セキュリティのビット数は \(\tau\) であり、任意の不正な暗号文が有効として受け入れられる確率の許容される最大値が \(2^{-\tau}\) であることを意味します。\(\tau\) の値は、暗号文の膨張の最小ビット数も示します。認証をサポートする派生関数は、\(\tau\) に許容される値の集合を指定し、その中に暗号文の膨張を小さくするオプションが含まれる場合があります。

contents.html: 4.4.2. Key and Context Commitment
contents.html_ja: 4.4.2. 鍵とコンテキストのコミットメント
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本の節見出し 4.4.x。level 4 に

contents.html: In many applications of cryptographic functions with authentication, it is important to have assurance that a given output can only be successfully authenticated when the key and other context (e.g., nonce and associated data) are correct (i.e., unchanged). In other words, it should be infeasible to find two different tuples of inputs that are cryptographically processed to the same output. This property is called key commitment when the key varies but the other context does not and context commitment when the key and other context may all vary.
contents.html_ja: 認証を伴う暗号関数の多くのアプリケーションでは、鍵とその他のコンテキスト（たとえば、ナンスと関連データ）が正しい（すなわち、変更されていない）場合にのみ、ある出力の認証が成功することの保証が重要です。言い換えれば、暗号処理して同じ出力になる、異なる 2 つの入力の組を見つけることは、計算上実行不可能であるべきです。この特性は、鍵が変化してその他のコンテキストは変化しない場合を鍵コミットメント、鍵とその他のコンテキストがすべて変化しうる場合をコンテキストコミットメントと呼びます。

contents.html: Formally, the “committing security” notions by Bellare and Hoang [45] are adapted: let \(C = F(K, P, U)\) be a derived function that processes key \(K\), (plaintext) message \(P\), and additional context \(U\) to produce (ciphertext) output \(C\). Key and context commitment are properties for which it should be computationally infeasible to find \(K_1, P_1, U_1, K_2, P_2\), and \(U_2\) such that \(F(K_1, P_1, U_1) = F(K_2, P_2, U_2)\). The key commitment property requires that \(K_1 \neq K_2\), while the context commitment property requires that \((K_1, P_1, U_1) \neq (K_2, P_2, U_2)\). For the AEAD derived function, this notion of key (context) commitment aligns with the definition in [45] for CMT-1 (CMT-4). Analogous definitions would apply for DAE and any other derived function with authentication.
contents.html_ja: 形式的には、Bellare と Hoang [45] による「コミットメントセキュリティ」の概念を適用します。\(C = F(K, P, U)\) を、鍵 \(K\)、（平文の）メッセージ \(P\)、追加のコンテキスト \(U\) を処理して（暗号文の）出力 \(C\) を生成する派生関数とします。鍵とコンテキストのコミットメントとは、\(K_1, P_1, U_1, K_2, P_2, U_2\) であって \(F(K_1, P_1, U_1) = F(K_2, P_2, U_2)\) となるものを見つけることが計算上実行不可能であるという特性です。鍵コミットメントの特性では \(K_1 \neq K_2\) を要求し、コンテキストコミットメントの特性では \((K_1, P_1, U_1) \neq (K_2, P_2, U_2)\) を要求します。AEAD 派生関数では、この鍵（コンテキスト）コミットメントの概念は、[45] における CMT-1（CMT-4）の定義に対応します。DAE や、認証を伴うその他の派生関数にも同様の定義が当てはまります。

contents.html: Because key commitment is important in many real-world applications, NIST expects to require this property in the derived functions that support authentication. Although context commitment would also be useful, it seems less essential and possibly more difficult to achieve. For this reason, NIST does not require context commitment but would consider designs that support this property.
contents.html_ja: 鍵コミットメントは多くの実世界のアプリケーションで重要であるため、NIST は、認証をサポートする派生関数にこの特性を求めることを見込んでいます。コンテキストコミットメントも有用ですが、重要性はやや低く、達成がより難しい可能性があります。このため、NIST はコンテキストコミットメントを求めませんが、この特性をサポートする設計は検討します。

contents.html: 4.4.3. Nonce Hiding

contents.html: In some applications that involve a cryptographic function with a nonce, the nonce may reveal private data and should not be disclosed. A function that protects the contents of the nonce from disclosure is said to be nonce-hiding [46]. It is straightforward to construct derived functions for AEAD with this property.
contents.html_ja: ナンスを伴う暗号関数を使うアプリケーションの一部では、ナンスが非公開のデータを明らかにする場合があり、開示すべきではありません。ナンスの内容を開示から保護する関数は、ナンス秘匿（nonce-hiding）であると言われます [46]。この特性を持つ AEAD の派生関数を構成するのは簡単です。

contents.html: 4.4.4. Release of Unverified Plaintext
contents.html_ja: 4.4.4. 未検証の平文の解放
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本の節見出し 4.4.x。level 4 に

contents.html: Cryptographic functions that provide authentication are subject to a particular kind of implementation failure: they can reveal plaintext before it has been authenticated. This is often difficult to avoid, especially when very large messages are being processed. Security under the release of unverified plaintext (RUP) is a property of a cryptographic function with authentication that ensures that the adversary does not gain an advantage if authentication fails, even if the unauthenticated plaintext is released. Several variations of this notion exist [47–50], the strongest of which requires leakage to be indistinguishable from random data. Using an encode-then-encipher approach for authenticated encryption over the accordion provides assurance of RUP security.
contents.html_ja: 認証を提供する暗号関数は、特有の種類の実装上の失敗を起こしえます。平文が認証される前に、それを明らかにしてしまう場合があります。これは、特に非常に大きなメッセージを処理している場合に、避けることが難しいことが多くあります。未検証の平文の解放（RUP）下でのセキュリティは、認証を伴う暗号関数の特性で、認証されていない平文が解放されたとしても、認証が失敗した場合に攻撃者が優位を得ないことを保証するものです。この概念にはいくつかの変種があり [47–50]、最も強いものは、漏えいがランダムなデータと区別できないことを求めます。アコーディオン上で認証付き暗号に encode-then-encipher アプローチを使うと、RUP セキュリティが保証されます。

ITL’s respon-sibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

The limitations of the current NIST modes were identified in NIST Internal Report (IR) 8459 [11] as part of NIST’s review process under the auspices of the NIST Crypto Publication Review Board.1 NIST hosted the Third Workshop on Block Cipher Modes of Operation 2023 2 to discuss how to improve NIST’s modes portfolio, including desirable additional security features and a variety of proposed techniques. As a follow up, NIST hosted the NIST Workshop on the Requirements for an Accordion Cipher Mode 2024 [12] to 1) propose the development of an accordion as a comprehensive solution for a variety of cryptographic functionalities and 2) solicit feedback on the design requirements.3

NIST has proposed to approve a block cipher with 256-bit blocks [43] and, therefore, ex-pects to develop an accordion with 𝑛 = 256. This main accordion, denoted by ACC256, would provide very high assurance against generic cryptanalytic attacks with relatively little performance overhead.
NIST requires any approved accordion to support 𝑘 = 256 and may also allow 𝑘 = 128 or 𝑘 = 192 for ACC128 or BBBACC.

While some 𝑚𝑎𝑥 applications (e.g., storage encryption) can take advantage of more efficient processing for tweaks that are short and of a fixed length, supporting fixed-length tweaks alone is insufficient. An accordion must be capable of handling the full range of required tweak lengths, even if it optimizes for specific, fixed-length tweaks to enhance performance in certain use cases. The ability to process variable-length tweaks remains essential to ensure flexibility and compatibility across diverse applications.

Given the granularity 𝑔, the minimum message bit length 𝑎𝑔, and the maximum message bit length 𝑏𝑔, an accordion supports a total of (𝑏 − 𝑎 + 1) allowed message lengths ℓ ∈ {𝑎𝑔,(𝑎 + 1)𝑔,…,𝑏𝑔}. An accordion with a granularity of one bit (𝑔 = 1) can process any message between its minimum and maximum length, whereas a scheme with a granularity of 128 bits can only process messages whose length is a multiple of 128 bits between its minimum and maximum lengths.

NIST requires a granularity of 𝑔 ≤ 8 and the minimum message length 𝑎𝑔 to be at most 2𝑛 bits for any accordion. NIST also requires the maximum message length to be at least 296 bits for ACC256, at least 248 bits for ACC128, and at least 264 bits for BBBACC.

This section describes the derived functions of an accordion for the following three cat-egories of applications: AEAD, tweakable encryption, and deterministic authenticated encryption (DAE). Each of these functions will have some application-specific inputs along with the message and a key. The particular use case of the function motivates a set of properties that should be achieved. For example, AEAD by definition includes a means of data authentication, while tweakable encryption does not. The following subsections provide 1) some guidelines for each of the derived functions, 2) an indication of how the functions could be constructed out of an accordion, and 3) discussion of additional security considerations.

An AEAD scheme uses a key, a nonce, and optional associated data to encrypt a plaintext into a ciphertext while authenticating the plaintext and associated data. One possible construction for authenticated encryption from an accordion is shown in Fig. 2. In this example, the accordion message consists of the plaintext padded with 𝜏 fixed bits (zeros) to support authentication5, which is verified upon decryption (not depicted). This construction encodes the nonce and any associated data into the accordion tweak.

In practice, it can be difficult to ensure that nonces are not repeated. Therefore, nonce misuse resistance is an important property for an AEAD scheme. If the nonce is encoded as part of the tweak, then the security definition of the accordion ensures that repetition of the tweak6 imposes the smallest possible security loss. Accordions are deterministic, so any invocations of the accordion on the same input — including the same tweak — will result in the same output. Otherwise, each new invocation will appear to be randomly selected from the set of not-yet-seen outputs of the correct length from the accordion function.

This report introduces the cryptographic accordion as a tweakable, variable-input-length strong pseudorandom permutation (VIL-SPRP) that is constructed from an underlying block cipher. An accordion facilitates the cryptographic processing of messages of various sizes while offering enhanced security compared to the approved block cipher modes of operation that are specified in the NIST SP 800-38 series. This report introduces associated terminology, outlines design requirements for accordions, and describes three categories of applications for them.

A mode of operation is a method that defines how a block cipher cryptographically processes (e.g., encrypts and/or authenticates) data beyond a single block length. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-38 series [2–10] specifies several modes that were submitted for NIST’s consideration from several different sources over many years to address a variety of security requirements and use cases.

NIST introduces the term cryptographic accordion — or simply accordion — to describe a technique constructed from an underlying block cipher that itself acts like a cipher on inputs of varying sizes. Thus, an accordion is simultaneously a cipher and a mode of the underlying block cipher. Formally, an accordion is defined as a tweakable, variable-input-length-strong pseudorandom permutation (VIL-SPRP) that is constructed from an underlying block cipher. NIST expects to develop one or more accordions with a generic proof of security.

In this report, the cryptographic functions that may be constructed from an accordion are called derived functions. These derived functions can use the properties of the accordion to offer improved security, usage bounds, and functionality over existing modes. For example, a derived function for authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) could provide additional security properties compared to Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) [6], such as nonce-misuse resistance, support for short tags, nonce hiding, and key commitment. These features could make the accordion-based derived function a more robust choice than GCM for many cryptographic applications.

Another benefit is that an accordion facilitates the conceptual separation of the enciphering from the functional roles of different types of inputs (e.g., confidential data, associated data, randomization values, and nonces). This separation should promote easier, faster, and simpler deployment compared to the ad hoc development of dedicated modes for specific functionalities and security features.

The notion of an accordion as a tweakable VIL-SPRP evolved from related terminology in the academic literature. The term strong pseudorandom permutation (SPRP) formally captures the idea that changing any bit of the input randomizes every bit of output for both the permutation and its inverse. The term enciphering mode describes a block cipher mode of operation that provides length-preserving encryption for variable input length (VIL) messages. The term tweakable enciphering mode indicates that the enciphering mode would take an additional input called a tweak, which was first introduced only in the context of a tweakable block cipher [13] (i.e., with fixed-length input).

Some early works are CMC [14], EME [15], and the Hasty Pudding Cipher [16]. Several related design approaches have since emerged, such as AEZ [17], HCTR2 [18], Glevian and Vigornian [19], and Docked Double Decker [20]. There are also constructions based on other primitives (e.g., XChacha [21]) and tweakable block ciphers (e.g., Adiantum [22] and ZCZ [23]). Bellare and Rogaway’s encode-then-encipher encryption [24] is an example of a technique that could be applied to an accordion to achieve authenticated encryption. Another category of techniques that support variable input lengths is format-preserving encryption (FPE), though the input domain is usually small in this case. Moreover, NIST’s standard FF1 [10] for FPE, although AES-based, is expected to perform much less efficiently than a well-designed accordion.
While none of the above designs may meet the exact requirements that are outlined in this document, they provide valuable background and reference material.

An accordion is one layer of a larger process for achieving a cryptographic functionality, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In particular, the underlying block cipher is the innermost layer, which is called by the accordion. The accordion is called by a derived function that defines how the accordion will be used but does not necessarily provide additional cryptographic processing of the inputs. For example, a derived function could provide AEAD functionality by encoding its inputs and providing them to the accordion. The derived function would then be called by an application, such as the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol for secure communication on the internet. One motivation for the development of an accordion is that it can support a variety of functionalities, which are currently met by ad hoc or dedicated modes of operation.

The usage bounds of many cryptographic techniques are limited by the “birthday bound,” where collisions (i.e., repetitions among a set of randomly generated data blocks) can be expected to occur. A technique that is specifically designed to provide “beyond-birthday-bound” (BBB) security against generic cryptanalytic attacks would support less restrictive usage bounds on the amount of data that is processed per key.

Security bounds for primitives (e.g., an accordion or derived function) are typically given for a single user. Multi-user security considers how the security of these primitives changes as the number of independent users of the primitive gets larger. There are generic bounds on multi-user security, but a complete analysis requires consideration of how a given construction of a primitive affects its multi-user security (e.g., [27–36]).

Evaluating how security degrades as the number of users grows is a challenging technical problem. While the generic bounds are acceptable, NIST prefers to standardize an accordion with better multi-user security than is provided by generic bounds.

Some applications involve encrypting inputs that include the key or are derived from the key in some way. For example, when the operating system swaps the contents of some memory page to disk, the storage encryption mode being used could encrypt a copy of its own key. The security proofs of most chaining modes do not cover this use case; the property required to ensure security is called security against key-dependent inputs (KDI security) [37–39]. As shown in [39], it is impossible to construct a KDI-secure deterministic construction (e.g., the accordion) if there is no restriction on generating KDIs.

However, it is expected that the typical application of an accordion for disk encryption will not have practical attacks in the KDI setting, as the attacks that were applicable to the initial drafts of the IEEE 1619 standard [11] are unlikely to apply to the setting where an accordion encrypts plaintexts whose size corresponds to an entire disk sector.

NIST is interested in both analysis and security proofs of the accordion in a quantum setting following the Q1 model [40–42], which assumes that a quantum adversary can only interact with the target primitive (i.e., make queries to Encrypt(T,x) and Decrypt(T,x)) through classical communication.

While performance is not as critical as security, the better an accordion performs, the more useful it is likely to be. The most important platform is likely to be relatively powerful processors in desktop or laptop computers and those used in cloud environments with hardware AES support. Performance in dedicated hardware, field programmable gate arrays, and constrained devices is also worthwhile but is not NIST’s focus for an accordion.

The security requirements for an accordion require multiple passes over the message. Thus, it is almost certain to be slower than many existing one-pass block cipher modes, like GCM. However, an accordion will ideally not be significantly more expensive than twice the cost (e.g., in time, block cipher calls, gates) of GCM over the same input size.

An accordion should allow substantial parallelism for large input sizes. Modern CPUs often support multiple AES instructions or other operations in parallel, and an accordion should allow the user to take advantage of this.

An accordion should not impose too much additional overhead on small input sizes. An accordion that does a substantial amount of setup work before processing an input block will generally perform poorly on small inputs. Some applications require efficient processing of even relatively short messages.

4.4. Security Properties of the Derived Functions

The derived functions should support each of the security properties described below to the highest extent reasonable. A specification of the derived functions should include analysis of the security goals and identify the level of security achieved for each.

In many applications of cryptographic functions with authentication, it is important to have assurance that a given output can only be successfully authenticated when the key and other context (e.g., nonce and associated data) are correct (i.e., unchanged). In other words, it should be infeasible to find two different tuples of inputs that are cryptographically processed to the same output. This property is called key commitment when the key varies but the other context does not and context commitment when the key and other context may all vary.

Because key commitment is important in many real-world applications, NIST expects to require this property in the derived functions that support authentication. Although context commitment would also be useful, it seems less essential and possibly more difficult to achieve. For this reason, NIST does not require context commitment but would consider designs that support this property.

In some applications that involve a cryptographic function with a nonce, the nonce may reveal private data and should not be disclosed. A function that protects the contents of the nonce from disclosure is said to be nonce-hiding [46]. It is straightforward to construct derived functions for AEAD with this property.

Cryptographic functions that provide authentication are subject to a particular kind of implementation failure: they can reveal plaintext before it has been authenticated. This is often difficult to avoid, especially when very large messages are being processed. Security under the release of unverified plaintext (RUP) is a property of a cryptographic function with authentication that ensures that the adversary does not gain an advantage if authentication fails, even if the unauthenticated plaintext is released. Several variations of this notion exist [47–50], the strongest of which requires leakage to be indistinguishable from random data. Using an encode-then-encipher approach for authenticated encryption over the accordion provides assurance of RUP security.

NIST intends to lead a collaborative, transparent process with the cryptographic community to develop accordions that are suitable for most general-purpose cryptographic applications, especially those that require confidentiality and/or authentication.

NIST expects to release a series of increasingly specific proposals for public feedback, beginning with a recommendation for a high-level design approach based on the current state of the art and ending with a full specification that meets the requirements in this publication.
